items.question_text: A healthy 6-year-old boy is having influenza vaccine for the first time this season. The parent was told that two doses are only for babies under 2, so one dose will do. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Give one double-strength dose
Give one dose this year and a second dose next year
Give one dose because he is over 2
Give two doses at least 4 weeks apart this season
Give two doses on the same day in different limbs
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Give two doses at least 4 weeks apart this season

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A school-aged child receiving influenza vaccine for the first time.

2. THE RULE
Children aged 6 months to under 9 years need two influenza doses at least 4 weeks apart in the first year they are vaccinated, then one dose each year.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends two doses of influenza vaccine, at least 4 weeks apart, for children aged 6 months to under 9 years in the first year they receive influenza vaccine. The 'under 2' rule is wrong.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Give one double-strength dose: Double doses are not used.
B. Give one dose this year and a second dose next year: The second dose belongs in the same season.
C. Give one dose because he is over 2: The two-dose rule extends to under 9 years.
E. Give two doses on the same day in different limbs: Two doses must be at least 4 weeks apart.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
First-year influenza vaccine under 9: two doses at least 4 weeks apart.

---

items.question_text: A 3-year-old Aboriginal girl is having a catch-up dose of meningococcal B vaccine. Her parent remembers being told to give paracetamol with MenB doses when she was a baby and asks whether to give it now. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Prophylactic paracetamol is not routinely needed at 3 years; treat fever if it occurs
Defer the vaccine until paracetamol is available
Give prophylactic ibuprofen instead
Give paracetamol 24 hours before the vaccine
Give prophylactic paracetamol, as for every MenB dose at any age
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Prophylactic paracetamol is not routinely needed at 3 years; treat fever if it occurs

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A child over 2 having MenB vaccine.

2. THE RULE
Prophylactic paracetamol is recommended with each MenB dose in children under 2 years, but is not routine for other vaccines.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Prophylactic paracetamol with MenB (Bexsero) is recommended for children under 2 years, because fever is common in that age group. It is not routinely recommended at 3 years; paracetamol can be given if fever occurs.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Defer the vaccine until paracetamol is available: Vaccination is not delayed for paracetamol.
C. Give prophylactic ibuprofen instead: Ibuprofen is not recommended as prophylaxis.
D. Give paracetamol 24 hours before the vaccine: Pre-dosing the day before is not recommended.
E. Give prophylactic paracetamol, as for every MenB dose at any age: The prophylaxis recommendation is age-limited to children under 2.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
MenB prophylactic paracetamol is for under 2 years, not older children.

---

items.question_text: In a residential aged care facility, two residents in the same wing develop vomiting and diarrhoea within 24 hours of each other. Both are otherwise stable. The manager says gastroenteritis is not notifiable, so no action outside the facility is needed. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Notify only if a resident dies
Treat it as a suspected gastroenteritis outbreak: start infection control and notify the public health unit
Transfer both residents to hospital to end the outbreak
Take no external action because single cases of gastroenteritis are not notifiable
Wait for stool PCR before telling anyone
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Treat it as a suspected gastroenteritis outbreak: start infection control and notify the public health unit

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Two linked gastroenteritis cases in aged care within 24 hours.

2. THE RULE
Notification follows the jurisdiction's notifiable disease list: a single mild community gastroenteritis is not notified, but suspected outbreaks such as linked childcare cases are.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
CDNA national guidelines for gastroenteritis in residential care define a suspected outbreak as two or more cases of diarrhoea and/or vomiting among residents or staff within 24 hours. Outbreaks are reported to the local public health unit and managed with infection control measures, even though individual cases of viral gastroenteritis are not notifiable.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Notify only if a resident dies: Waiting for a death misses the point of outbreak control.
C. Transfer both residents to hospital to end the outbreak: Transfer does not control an outbreak and may spread it.
D. Take no external action because single cases of gastroenteritis are not notifiable: Outbreak reporting is separate from single-case notification.
E. Wait for stool PCR before telling anyone: Outbreak control and reporting start on suspicion, not after pathology.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Two or more linked gastro cases within 24 h in aged care: suspected outbreak, notify public health.

---

items.question_text: A 20-year-old woman with HIV (CD4 count 280 cells/µL) has never had HPV vaccine. A colleague advises a single dose, as for other young people. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Defer vaccination until her CD4 count is above 500
Give two doses 6 months apart
HPV vaccine is contraindicated in HIV
Give a three-dose course (0, 2 and 6 months)
Give a single dose
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Give a three-dose course (0, 2 and 6 months)

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
An immunocompromised young adult needing HPV vaccine.

2. THE RULE
Routine adolescent HPV vaccination is a single dose, with funded catch-up available up to age 25.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends a three-dose HPV vaccine course (0, 2 and 6 months) for people who are significantly immunocompromised, including people living with HIV. The single-dose schedule applies to immunocompetent people.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Defer vaccination until her CD4 count is above 500: Vaccination is not deferred for CD4 count.
B. Give two doses 6 months apart: Two doses are not the recommended schedule for immunocompromised people.
C. HPV vaccine is contraindicated in HIV: HPV vaccine is non-live and safe in HIV.
E. Give a single dose: The single-dose schedule is for immunocompetent people.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Immunocompromised people need three HPV doses, not one.

---

items.question_text: A family has moved from New Zealand with a written record of their 4-year-old's vaccines. The AIR shows no doses, so Services Australia lists him as overdue. The parent asks if he must repeat all the vaccines. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Write a letter to Services Australia instead of updating the AIR
Leave him listed as overdue because overseas doses cannot be recorded
A recognised vaccination provider records the documented overseas doses on the AIR
Ask the parent to upload the record to the AIR themselves
Repeat all the vaccines so the AIR shows them
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. A recognised vaccination provider records the documented overseas doses on the AIR

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A child with documented overseas vaccines not on the AIR.

2. THE RULE
Missing vaccination records are fixed by a recognised vaccination provider submitting the encounter to the AIR with the actual date given.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Vaccines given overseas can be recorded on the AIR by a recognised vaccination provider after reviewing the documented history. This updates the child's status. Valid documented doses are counted and are not repeated.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Write a letter to Services Australia instead of updating the AIR: A letter does not change the AIR status.
B. Leave him listed as overdue because overseas doses cannot be recorded: Documented overseas vaccines can be recorded on the AIR.
D. Ask the parent to upload the record to the AIR themselves: Parents cannot enter clinical vaccination records on the AIR.
E. Repeat all the vaccines so the AIR shows them: Repeating valid documented doses is unnecessary.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Recognised providers record documented overseas doses on the AIR.

---

items.question_text: A 41-year-old Aboriginal woman had an MBS 715 health assessment 10 months ago. She attends as an outpatient and asks for her next one. The practice manager says another 715 cannot be claimed until 12 months have passed. What is the most appropriate response?
options: She can have the 715 now, because the minimum interval is 9 months
She must wait 2 years, as for adult health assessments
A 715 can only be claimed once in a lifetime
She must wait until 12 months have passed
She needs a specialist referral before a repeat 715
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. She can have the 715 now, because the minimum interval is 9 months

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A repeat 715 request 10 months after the last one.

2. THE RULE
The MBS 715 health assessment is offered on self-identification as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, at least 9 months apart, to a non-admitted patient, never to a hospital inpatient.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
MBS item 715 can be claimed for an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander patient no more often than once every 9 months. At 10 months she is eligible now. The patient is non-admitted, so the inpatient exclusion does not apply.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. She must wait 2 years, as for adult health assessments: There is no 2-year interval for 715.
C. A 715 can only be claimed once in a lifetime: The 715 is repeated at least 9 months apart, not once only.
D. She must wait until 12 months have passed: The interval is 9 months, not 12.
E. She needs a specialist referral before a repeat 715: No referral is needed for a 715.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
A 715 can be repeated after 9 months.

---

items.question_text: A 58-year-old Torres Strait Islander man was registered for Closing the Gap PBS co-payment relief by his GP in Cairns last year. He has moved to Adelaide, sees a new GP, and is told he must re-register with the new practice before the CTG benefit applies. What is the most appropriate response?
options: He loses eligibility when he leaves a remote area
He must re-register with each new practice
He must re-register every 12 months
His registration is national and one-off; he does not need to re-register
Only an Aboriginal community controlled service in Adelaide can restore it
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. His registration is national and one-off; he does not need to re-register

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A registered patient moves interstate and is told to re-register.

2. THE RULE
Closing the Gap PBS co-payment relief needs a one-off registration by a PBS prescriber or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Practitioner; writing CTG on a script (optional since July 2021) or asking a pharmacist does not create eligibility.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Since 1 July 2021, CTG PBS co-payment registration is a one-off registration recorded with Services Australia and applies nationally at any pharmacy, so it continues after a move. It no longer has to be renewed with each practice or each year.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. He loses eligibility when he leaves a remote area: CTG eligibility is not limited to remote areas.
B. He must re-register with each new practice: Registration is linked to the patient, not the practice.
C. He must re-register every 12 months: There is no annual renewal.
E. Only an Aboriginal community controlled service in Adelaide can restore it: Any PBS prescriber's earlier registration stays valid.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
CTG PBS registration is one-off and national.

---

items.question_text: A 12-year-old Aboriginal girl in a remote Northern Territory community has a single hot, swollen knee and fever of 38.4°C. CRP is 90 mg/L. A sore throat 3 weeks ago was not treated. A registrar says ARF needs polyarthritis, so this is septic arthritis or a sprain. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Wait for a migratory pattern to develop before considering ARF
Treat as possible ARF: arrange echocardiography and joint assessment, notify, and add to the RHD register if confirmed
Give oral antibiotics and review in a month
Diagnose a sprain and give NSAIDs only
Exclude ARF because there is only one joint
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Treat as possible ARF: arrange echocardiography and joint assessment, notify, and add to the RHD register if confirmed

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A high-risk child with monoarthritis after an untreated sore throat.

2. THE RULE
Suspected acute rheumatic fever needs echocardiography, notification and referral to the RHD register.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Under the Australian ARF/RHD guideline, in high-risk populations monoarthritis (and polyarthralgia) counts as a major manifestation, because ARF commonly presents this way. Septic arthritis must still be excluded. The child needs echocardiography, notification and register referral if ARF is diagnosed. NSAIDs can mask the migratory pattern and are best held until the diagnosis is clear.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Wait for a migratory pattern to develop before considering ARF: Waiting for migration, especially on NSAIDs, delays diagnosis.
C. Give oral antibiotics and review in a month: Delay misses carditis and the start of secondary prophylaxis.
D. Diagnose a sprain and give NSAIDs only: A missed diagnosis of ARF or septic arthritis is the risk here.
E. Exclude ARF because there is only one joint: Monoarthritis is a major criterion in high-risk groups.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
In high-risk groups, monoarthritis can be a major criterion for ARF.

---

items.question_text: A 10-year-old Aboriginal boy has 3 weeks of jerky, involuntary movements of his arms and face, with clumsy handwriting. He has no fever, joint symptoms or murmur, and his CRP is normal. A colleague says ARF cannot be diagnosed without raised inflammatory markers. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose a tic disorder and reassure
Exclude ARF because inflammatory markers are normal
Consider Sydenham chorea as ARF: arrange echocardiography, notify, and start secondary prophylaxis if confirmed
Repeat the CRP in a month before acting
Refer to neurology only, as ARF is not relevant
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Consider Sydenham chorea as ARF: arrange echocardiography, notify, and start secondary prophylaxis if confirmed

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A high-risk child with isolated chorea and normal inflammatory markers.

2. THE RULE
Suspected acute rheumatic fever needs echocardiography, notification and referral to the RHD register.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Sydenham chorea is a major manifestation that can occur months after the streptococcal infection, often when inflammatory markers have returned to normal. Once other causes are excluded, chorea alone can establish ARF in the Australian guideline. Echocardiography is needed because subclinical carditis is common.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Diagnose a tic disorder and reassure: Chorea in a high-risk child should not be dismissed as tics.
B. Exclude ARF because inflammatory markers are normal: Normal markers are expected in late-onset chorea.
D. Repeat the CRP in a month before acting: Delay misses carditis and secondary prophylaxis.
E. Refer to neurology only, as ARF is not relevant: Chorea is an ARF manifestation; the cardiac risk must be assessed.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Sydenham chorea can establish ARF even with normal inflammatory markers.

---

items.question_text: A 45-year-old man who came to Australia as a refugee from Myanmar 4 years ago has newly diagnosed polymyalgia-like symptoms, and the rheumatologist plans prednisolone 15 mg daily for many months. His eosinophil count is normal and he has no gut symptoms. What is the most appropriate step before starting steroids?
options: Test for Strongyloides serology and treat with ivermectin if positive, or give empirical ivermectin if steroids cannot wait
Check a single stool microscopy and proceed if negative
Only screen people from remote northern Australia
Start steroids; a normal eosinophil count excludes Strongyloides
Give albendazole once and start steroids
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Test for Strongyloides serology and treat with ivermectin if positive, or give empirical ivermectin if steroids cannot wait

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A migrant from an endemic region about to start long-term steroids.

2. THE RULE
Before corticosteroids or immunosuppression in a person from a Strongyloides-endemic setting, check serology or give pre-emptive ivermectin.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Strongyloides is endemic in South-East Asia as well as remote northern Australia. People from endemic areas should have serology (or empirical ivermectin) before steroids, because the infection can persist for decades and cause hyperinfection when immunosuppressed. Eosinophil counts and stool microscopy are insensitive.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Check a single stool microscopy and proceed if negative: Single stool microscopy has poor sensitivity.
C. Only screen people from remote northern Australia: Refugees and migrants from endemic regions are also at risk.
D. Start steroids; a normal eosinophil count excludes Strongyloides: A normal eosinophil count does not exclude chronic infection.
E. Give albendazole once and start steroids: Ivermectin, not albendazole, is the treatment of choice.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Screen or treat for Strongyloides before steroids in anyone from an endemic region.

---

items.question_text: A 60-year-old man from a remote Kimberley community has been on high-dose dexamethasone for 2 weeks for spinal cord compression from a lymphoma. He now has fever, abdominal pain, diffuse wheeze and Gram-negative bacteraemia (E. coli). He has never had Strongyloides testing. What is the most important additional diagnosis to consider and treat?
options: Lymphoma progression: start chemotherapy now
Steroid-induced asthma: increase the dexamethasone
Strongyloides hyperinfection: give ivermectin urgently and reduce steroids if possible
Simple E. coli urinary sepsis: antibiotics alone
Drug fever from dexamethasone: stop all medications
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Strongyloides hyperinfection: give ivermectin urgently and reduce steroids if possible

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A steroid-treated man from an endemic area with Gram-negative sepsis.

2. THE RULE
Before corticosteroids or immunosuppression in a person from a Strongyloides-endemic setting, check serology or give pre-emptive ivermectin.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Gram-negative bacteraemia with respiratory and gut symptoms in a steroid-treated person from an endemic area suggests Strongyloides hyperinfection. Larvae carry gut bacteria into the blood. It is often fatal unless treated urgently with ivermectin, with infectious diseases input, alongside antibiotics and a reduction in immunosuppression where possible.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Lymphoma progression: start chemotherapy now: Chemotherapy would worsen immunosuppression before the infection is treated.
B. Steroid-induced asthma: increase the dexamethasone: More steroid worsens hyperinfection.
D. Simple E. coli urinary sepsis: antibiotics alone: Antibiotics alone miss the cause of the bacteraemia.
E. Drug fever from dexamethasone: stop all medications: Stopping all drugs, including antibiotics, is unsafe.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Gram-negative sepsis on steroids in an endemic patient: think Strongyloides hyperinfection.

---

items.question_text: A 52-year-old woman with diabetes in Darwin has had 2 weeks of IV meropenem for culture-confirmed melioidosis pneumonia. She is now afebrile and well. The team plans to discharge her with no further antibiotics. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Give 7 days of oral amoxicillin
Start oral eradication therapy with co-trimoxazole for at least 3 months
Continue IV meropenem for 6 more months
Give a single dose of benzathine penicillin
Discharge with no further antibiotics
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Start oral eradication therapy with co-trimoxazole for at least 3 months

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Melioidosis after completion of IV intensive therapy.

2. THE RULE
Suspected melioidosis in tropical northern Australia is treated with IV ceftazidime or meropenem, not standard community pneumonia antibiotics.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Melioidosis is treated in two phases: an intensive IV phase (ceftazidime or meropenem) followed by an eradication phase, usually oral co-trimoxazole for at least 3 months, to reduce relapse. Stopping after IV therapy alone carries a high relapse risk.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Give 7 days of oral amoxicillin: Amoxicillin is not an effective eradication regimen.
C. Continue IV meropenem for 6 more months: Long-term IV therapy is not needed once the intensive phase is complete.
D. Give a single dose of benzathine penicillin: Benzathine penicillin has no role in melioidosis.
E. Discharge with no further antibiotics: Omitting eradication therapy increases relapse.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Melioidosis needs IV intensive therapy, then at least 3 months of oral co-trimoxazole.

---

items.question_text: During ED registration, a 37-year-old man is asked the standard question about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander origin. He says he would rather not answer. The clerk plans to mark him as 'non-Indigenous' so the field is not blank. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Record 'not stated' and respect his choice; he can be asked again in future
Record 'Aboriginal' based on his surname
Record 'non-Indigenous' so the field is complete
Refuse registration until he answers
Ask him for proof of Aboriginality
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Record 'not stated' and respect his choice; he can be asked again in future

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A patient declines to answer the Indigenous status question.

2. THE RULE
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status is recorded from the person's own answer to the standard question, asked of every patient, and never assumed from appearance or required to be proven.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
The Indigenous status question is voluntary. If a person declines or does not answer, the response is recorded as 'not stated/inadequately described'. A status is never assumed or guessed from appearance, name or other cues, and no proof is required.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Record 'Aboriginal' based on his surname: Surnames are not a basis for Indigenous status.
C. Record 'non-Indigenous' so the field is complete: Recording a status he did not give corrupts the data.
D. Refuse registration until he answers: Care cannot be made conditional on answering.
E. Ask him for proof of Aboriginality: Proof of Aboriginality is never required for health records.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
If a person declines, record 'not stated'; never assume.

---

items.question_text: A 26-year-old Aboriginal woman with rheumatic heart disease and a mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin. A home pregnancy test is positive and she is about 6 weeks pregnant. She feels well and her next cardiology review is in 4 months. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Book routine low-risk midwifery care
Switch to a direct oral anticoagulant
Stop warfarin today with no replacement
Arrange urgent specialist review (obstetric medicine and cardiology) now to plan anticoagulation
Keep her on warfarin and review at the booked cardiology visit
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Arrange urgent specialist review (obstetric medicine and cardiology) now to plan anticoagulation

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Early pregnancy in a woman with a mechanical valve on warfarin.

2. THE RULE
A pregnant woman with known RHD needs shared specialist obstetric and cardiac care and continued secondary prophylaxis, not routine low-risk care.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
A mechanical valve in pregnancy is very high risk. Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester (especially weeks 6 to 12), but stopping anticoagulation risks valve thrombosis. She needs urgent multidisciplinary specialist planning about warfarin versus LMWH, while secondary prophylaxis continues.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Book routine low-risk midwifery care: Routine low-risk care is unsafe with RHD and a mechanical valve.
B. Switch to a direct oral anticoagulant: DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical valves.
C. Stop warfarin today with no replacement: Stopping anticoagulation risks valve thrombosis.
E. Keep her on warfarin and review at the booked cardiology visit: Waiting 4 months passes the critical embryopathy window.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Mechanical valve plus pregnancy: urgent specialist planning, never routine care.

---

items.question_text: A 64-year-old man in a remote community has thick, crusted, scaly plaques on his hands and back with little itch. Several family members and visiting health workers now have itchy rashes. Skin scrapings show many mites. The nurse plans a single permethrin application for him and his household. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Treat as crusted scabies: repeated oral ivermectin plus topical scabicide and keratolytic, specialist input, and treatment of all contacts
A single permethrin application for him and the household
Permethrin for him alone, as contacts have only a hypersensitivity rash
Oral antibiotics only
Topical steroid for presumed psoriasis
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Treat as crusted scabies: repeated oral ivermectin plus topical scabicide and keratolytic, specialist input, and treatment of all contacts

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Crusted scabies in an older man with symptomatic contacts.

2. THE RULE
Scabies is treated in the whole household at the same time, with impetigo treated alongside, not just the index child.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Crusted scabies involves a very high mite load and is highly contagious. It needs multiple doses of oral ivermectin with topical permethrin and keratolytic therapy, usually with hospital or specialist involvement, and screening and treatment of all contacts. In the Northern Territory it is notifiable. A single permethrin application is inadequate.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. A single permethrin application for him and the household: One application of permethrin fails in crusted scabies.
C. Permethrin for him alone, as contacts have only a hypersensitivity rash: Contacts need treatment because transmission is high.
D. Oral antibiotics only: Antibiotics treat secondary infection only.
E. Topical steroid for presumed psoriasis: Steroids will worsen scabies.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Crusted scabies needs repeated ivermectin plus topical therapy and contact treatment.

---

items.question_text: A 58-year-old Aboriginal man with an infected diabetic foot wound needs IV antibiotics for a week. A close relative has just died, and he says he must return to his community for sorry business and will leave today. He has capacity. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Refuse to discuss sorry business as it is not a medical issue
Ask security to keep him on the ward
Involve the Aboriginal Liaison Officer to plan care that allows him to attend, such as early follow-up, oral or outreach therapy, with risks explained
Stop his antibiotics because he is leaving
Tell him he will be discharged against medical advice and give no plan
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Involve the Aboriginal Liaison Officer to plan care that allows him to attend, such as early follow-up, oral or outreach therapy, with risks explained

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A patient needing IV antibiotics wants to leave for sorry business.

2. THE RULE
Culturally safe care follows the patient's wishes about family and Aboriginal Health Workers but never replaces or delays clinical assessment, and symptoms are not attributed to stereotypes.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Culturally safe care recognises the importance of sorry business and works with the patient, the Aboriginal Liaison Officer and the community health service to find a safe plan, such as oral antibiotics, outreach care and a planned return, while explaining the clinical risks. A person with capacity cannot be detained.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Refuse to discuss sorry business as it is not a medical issue: Dismissing cultural obligations undermines trust and engagement.
B. Ask security to keep him on the ward: A competent adult cannot be detained to receive treatment.
D. Stop his antibiotics because he is leaving: Stopping treatment is unsafe when alternatives exist.
E. Tell him he will be discharged against medical advice and give no plan: Leaving him without a plan increases harm.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Plan care around cultural obligations with the ALO rather than forcing a choice.

---

items.question_text: A trachoma-endemic community has had azithromycin mass drug administration twice, but child prevalence remains high. Many children have dirty faces with flies around their eyes, and several houses lack working taps. The visiting team plans a third antibiotic round only. What is the most appropriate addition?
options: Stop antibiotics because they have failed
Switch to topical chloramphenicol drops for every child
Refer every child for eyelid surgery
Strengthen facial cleanliness and environmental improvement (working washing facilities) alongside antibiotics
Screen only adults for trichiasis
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Strengthen facial cleanliness and environmental improvement (working washing facilities) alongside antibiotics

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Persistent trachoma despite antibiotic rounds.

2. THE RULE
Trachoma in an endemic community is managed with the SAFE strategy (surgery, antibiotics, facial cleanliness, environmental improvement).

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
The SAFE strategy combines Surgery for trichiasis, Antibiotics, Facial cleanliness and Environmental improvement. Antibiotics alone do not stop reinfection when face washing and functioning washing facilities are lacking.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Stop antibiotics because they have failed: Antibiotics remain part of SAFE; the missing parts must be added.
B. Switch to topical chloramphenicol drops for every child: Topical drops are not the community control approach.
C. Refer every child for eyelid surgery: Surgery is for trichiasis, not active trachoma.
E. Screen only adults for trichiasis: Children are the main reservoir of active trachoma.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
SAFE needs facial cleanliness and environment, not antibiotics alone.

---

items.question_text: A 4-year-old Aboriginal boy has a 715 health assessment. His immunisation record on the AIR shows he missed his 18-month vaccines and his 4-year vaccines are due. He is well today. His parent is happy to proceed. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Note the gap and wait until the next 715 in 9 months
Refer to a paediatrician before any vaccine is given
Restart the whole childhood schedule
Tell the parent the missed 18-month vaccines can no longer be given
Give the due and catch-up vaccines today if appropriate and record a follow-up plan
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Give the due and catch-up vaccines today if appropriate and record a follow-up plan

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Missed vaccinations found at a child's 715.

2. THE RULE
Problems found at a 715 health assessment need an arranged follow-up plan, using post-assessment nurse/Aboriginal Health Practitioner and allied health follow-up items, not the next health check.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
A 715 health assessment is an opportunity to act on gaps found. Catch-up vaccination should start at the visit, using all documented doses and the minimum intervals, with the plan recorded and follow-up arranged.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Note the gap and wait until the next 715 in 9 months: Waiting for the next assessment leaves him unprotected.
B. Refer to a paediatrician before any vaccine is given: A well child does not need specialist review before catch-up.
C. Restart the whole childhood schedule: The schedule is never restarted.
D. Tell the parent the missed 18-month vaccines can no longer be given: Missed doses are caught up, not abandoned.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Gaps found at a 715 are acted on with a follow-up plan, such as catch-up vaccination.

---

items.question_text: A 6-year-old Aboriginal girl in a remote community has three crusted, purulent skin sores on her legs. She is otherwise well. The nurse plans topical mupirocin because the sores are small. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Wash with soap and review in 2 weeks
Systemic treatment: oral co-trimoxazole for 3 to 5 days, or a single IM benzathine benzylpenicillin dose
Oral amoxicillin for 1 day
Topical mupirocin
Topical steroid cream
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Systemic treatment: oral co-trimoxazole for 3 to 5 days, or a single IM benzathine benzylpenicillin dose

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Impetigo in a child in a high-risk community.

2. THE RULE
In populations at high risk of rheumatic fever, sore throats (ages 3-35) and skin sores are treated promptly as streptococcal, e.g. IM benzathine benzylpenicillin G or 10 days of amoxicillin, without waiting for swab results.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
In high-risk Aboriginal communities, impetigo (skin sores) is treated systemically, with oral co-trimoxazole for 3 to 5 days or IM benzathine benzylpenicillin, to clear Streptococcus pyogenes and reduce the risk of APSGN and probably ARF. Topical antibiotics are not recommended in this setting because of resistance and poor efficacy.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Wash with soap and review in 2 weeks: Hygiene alone does not treat streptococcal skin infection.
C. Oral amoxicillin for 1 day: A single day of amoxicillin is inadequate.
D. Topical mupirocin: Topical mupirocin is not recommended for impetigo in high-risk communities.
E. Topical steroid cream: Steroids may worsen infection.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
High-risk impetigo is treated systemically, not with topical antibiotics.

---

items.question_text: A 7-year-old boy in a remote community has had a discharging ear with a perforated drum for 3 months. The clinic plans oral amoxicillin and asks the family to keep the ear dry until the next visit in 6 weeks. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Regular ear toilet (dry mopping or syringing) followed by topical ciprofloxacin drops, with hearing assessment
Advise that the perforation will heal without treatment
Refer for grommets
Aminoglycoside ear drops
Oral amoxicillin and review in 6 weeks
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Regular ear toilet (dry mopping or syringing) followed by topical ciprofloxacin drops, with hearing assessment

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Chronic ear discharge through a perforation in a remote child.

2. THE RULE
Chronic suppurative otitis media in a remote child is actively treated with ear cleaning and topical antibiotics and the hearing is formally assessed.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
CSOM (discharge through a perforation for more than 6 weeks) is treated with frequent ear cleaning followed by topical ciprofloxacin drops, continued until the ear is dry, with follow-up and hearing assessment. Oral antibiotics alone are less effective. Ciprofloxacin is preferred because aminoglycoside drops carry a risk of ototoxicity with a perforated drum.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Advise that the perforation will heal without treatment: Untreated CSOM causes hearing loss and complications.
C. Refer for grommets: Grommets are not the treatment for an existing perforation.
D. Aminoglycoside ear drops: Aminoglycoside drops risk ototoxicity with a perforated drum.
E. Oral amoxicillin and review in 6 weeks: Oral antibiotics alone are less effective than ear toilet plus topical quinolone.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
CSOM: ear toilet plus topical ciprofloxacin, with hearing assessment.

---

items.question_text: A 32-year-old Aboriginal man attends for a health check. He smokes and his blood pressure is 138/86 mmHg. He has no known heart disease. A registrar, using the old 2012 guideline, says formal cardiovascular risk assessment starts at 35 for Aboriginal people. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Wait until he is 45, as for the general population
Wait until he is 35
Assess his cardiovascular risk now; the 2023 guideline recommends assessment from 30 years for First Nations people
Assess risk only if he has diabetes
Assess risk only after a cardiac event
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Assess his cardiovascular risk now; the 2023 guideline recommends assessment from 30 years for First Nations people

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A 32-year-old Aboriginal smoker at a health check.

2. THE RULE
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults have cardiovascular risk assessed from 30 years, and standard calculators may underestimate their risk.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
The 2023 Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk recommends assessment from 30 years for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people (compared with 45 to 79 in the general population), using the Aus CVD Risk Calculator with recalibration as advised. The previous guideline started at 35.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Wait until he is 45, as for the general population: 45 applies to the general population.
B. Wait until he is 35: 35 was the previous recommendation, now replaced.
D. Assess risk only if he has diabetes: Assessment does not depend on diabetes.
E. Assess risk only after a cardiac event: Waiting for an event defeats primary prevention.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
From 2023, First Nations CVD risk assessment starts at 30.

---

items.question_text: A 44-year-old Aboriginal woman has diabetes and chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 40 mL/min/1.73 m² and persistent albuminuria. A registrar enters her details into the risk calculator, gets a moderate 5-year risk, and plans lifestyle advice alone. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Use a standard calculator without adjustment
She is at high risk on clinical criteria, so the calculator is not needed and treatment should be intensified
Rely on the calculator: moderate risk means lifestyle advice only
Cardiovascular risk cannot be assessed until she is 45
Repeat the calculator in 5 years
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. She is at high risk on clinical criteria, so the calculator is not needed and treatment should be intensified

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A First Nations woman with CKD and a moderate calculator score.

2. THE RULE
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults have cardiovascular risk assessed from 30 years, and standard calculators may underestimate their risk.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
The 2023 Australian guideline lists conditions that place people at high cardiovascular risk without calculation, including moderate to severe chronic kidney disease (such as eGFR below 45 or persistent significant albuminuria). These people need full risk-reducing treatment, including lipid and blood pressure management.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Use a standard calculator without adjustment: Standard tools underestimate First Nations risk.
C. Rely on the calculator: moderate risk means lifestyle advice only: A calculator underestimates risk in people already at high clinical risk.
D. Cardiovascular risk cannot be assessed until she is 45: First Nations assessment starts from 30.
E. Repeat the calculator in 5 years: Waiting 5 years leaves high risk untreated.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Clinically high-risk conditions such as moderate to severe CKD need no calculator.

---

items.question_text: A rapid test for a respiratory infection has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 80%. A patient with a pre-test probability of 20% tests negative. A student wants the negative likelihood ratio to update the probability. What is the negative likelihood ratio?
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. 0.125

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Calculating a negative likelihood ratio.

2. THE RULE
Sensitivity and specificity are test properties; a negative highly sensitive test helps rule disease out, and the post-test probability also needs prevalence or likelihood ratios.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
The negative likelihood ratio is (1 − sensitivity) / specificity = 0.10 / 0.80 = 0.125. A value well below 1 means a negative result lowers the probability of disease.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. 4.5: 4.5 is the positive likelihood ratio, sensitivity / (1 − specificity).
B. 0.2: 0.2 is 1 − specificity, the false-positive rate.
C. 8: 8 is the reciprocal of the negative likelihood ratio.
E. 0.9: 0.9 is the sensitivity.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity.

---

items.question_text: A test with a sensitivity of 80% and a specificity of 90% is used in a clinic where 50% of those tested have the disease. Of 1000 people tested, what is the negative predictive value?
options: About 89%
About 82%
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. About 82%

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
NPV calculation at 50% prevalence.

2. THE RULE
Positive predictive value depends on prevalence: with fixed sensitivity and specificity it falls as prevalence falls, so most positives may be false in a low-prevalence population.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
With 500 diseased: 400 true positives and 100 false negatives. With 500 non-diseased: 450 true negatives and 50 false positives. NPV = TN / (TN + FN) = 450 / 550 ≈ 82%. PPV would be 400 / 450 ≈ 89%.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. 80%: 80% is the sensitivity.
B. 90%: 90% is the specificity, not the NPV.
C. About 89%: About 89% is the positive predictive value.
D. 50%: 50% is the prevalence.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
NPV = true negatives / all negatives; it depends on prevalence.

---

items.question_text: A program screens for a disease with a prevalence of 0.5%. Most positive results are false positives. The board can fund one improvement: raising sensitivity from 90% to 99%, or raising specificity from 95% to 99.5%. Which improvement would increase the positive predictive value most?
options: Raising sensitivity, because it reduces false negatives
Neither, because PPV depends only on prevalence
Both have the same effect on PPV
Raising sensitivity to 99%
Raising specificity to 99.5%
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Raising specificity to 99.5%

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Improving PPV in a low-prevalence screening program.

2. THE RULE
Positive predictive value depends on prevalence: with fixed sensitivity and specificity it falls as prevalence falls, so most positives may be false in a low-prevalence population.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
At low prevalence, most positives come from the large non-diseased group, so false positives drive PPV. Per 10,000 people (50 diseased): with specificity 95%, about 498 false positives, PPV ≈ 45/543 ≈ 8%; with specificity 99.5%, about 50 false positives, PPV ≈ 45/95 ≈ 47%. Raising sensitivity adds only about 4 true positives.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Raising sensitivity, because it reduces false negatives: Fewer false negatives improves NPV, not PPV.
B. Neither, because PPV depends only on prevalence: PPV depends on sensitivity, specificity and prevalence.
C. Both have the same effect on PPV: The effects differ greatly at low prevalence.
D. Raising sensitivity to 99%: Higher sensitivity adds few true positives when the disease is rare.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
At low prevalence, specificity drives PPV.

---

items.question_text: In a stable population, a chronic disease has an incidence of 2 per 1000 per year and an average duration of 10 years. A new treatment prolongs survival without curing the disease, doubling the average duration. Incidence is unchanged. What happens to prevalence?
options: Prevalence roughly doubles, from about 20 to about 40 per 1000
Prevalence falls because the treatment works
Incidence doubles
Prevalence halves
Prevalence is unchanged because incidence is unchanged
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Prevalence roughly doubles, from about 20 to about 40 per 1000

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A life-prolonging treatment for an incurable disease.

2. THE RULE
Incidence is new cases in a population over a period of time, while prevalence is all existing cases at a point in time.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
In a steady state, prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration. 2 per 1000 per year × 10 years ≈ 20 per 1000; doubling duration to 20 years gives about 40 per 1000. Treatments that prolong life without cure raise prevalence.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Prevalence falls because the treatment works: Prolonging survival without cure increases prevalence.
C. Incidence doubles: Incidence (new cases) is unchanged by treatment.
D. Prevalence halves: Longer duration raises prevalence; it does not halve it.
E. Prevalence is unchanged because incidence is unchanged: Prevalence depends on duration as well as incidence.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration.

---

items.question_text: A town has 10,000 residents. At 1 January, 500 have type 2 diabetes. During the year, 95 new cases are diagnosed. A student calculates incidence as 95/10,000. What is the correct annual incidence (risk) of type 2 diabetes?
options: 95/9500, which is 1%
95/500, which is 19%
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. 95/9500, which is 1%

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Calculating incidence with the correct denominator.

2. THE RULE
Incidence is new cases in a population over a period of time, while prevalence is all existing cases at a point in time.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Incidence counts new cases among people at risk. The 500 people with existing diabetes cannot become new cases, so the population at risk is 9500. 95/9500 = 1%.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. 95/10,000, which is 0.95%: The denominator must exclude existing cases.
C. 500/10,000, which is 5%: 500/10,000 is the prevalence at 1 January.
D. 595/10,000, which is 5.95%: This adds prevalent and incident cases together.
E. 95/500, which is 19%: Existing cases are not the population at risk.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Incidence uses the population at risk as the denominator.

---

items.question_text: In a trial, major bleeding occurred in 3% of patients on a new anticoagulant and 1% on placebo. A patient asks how many people would need to take the drug for one extra major bleed. What is the number needed to harm?
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. 50

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Calculating number needed to harm.

2. THE RULE
The number needed to treat is 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction, and relative risk reductions overstate small absolute benefits.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
The absolute risk increase is 3% − 1% = 2 percentage points (0.02). NNH = 1 / 0.02 = 50.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. 33: 33 is 1/0.03, using only the treated group risk.
B. 200: 200 is not derived from these figures.
C. 2: 2 is the absolute difference in percentage points.
E. 100: 100 is 1/0.01, using only the placebo risk.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
NNH = 1 / absolute risk increase.

---

items.question_text: A trial reports that a drug reduces the 5-year risk of stroke from 20% to 15%. A drug company leaflet headlines the relative risk reduction. What are the relative risk reduction and the absolute risk reduction?
options: RRR 5%, ARR 25%
RRR 75%, ARR 5%
RRR 25%, ARR 5%
RRR 25%, ARR 15%
RRR 33%, ARR 5%
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. RRR 25%, ARR 5%

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Separating relative and absolute risk reduction.

2. THE RULE
The number needed to treat is 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction, and relative risk reductions overstate small absolute benefits.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
ARR = 20% − 15% = 5 percentage points. RRR = ARR / control risk = 5/20 = 25%. The NNT over 5 years is 1/0.05 = 20.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. RRR 5%, ARR 25%: This reverses the two measures.
B. RRR 75%, ARR 5%: 75% is the relative risk (15/20), not the reduction.
D. RRR 25%, ARR 15%: 15% is the treated group's risk.
E. RRR 33%, ARR 5%: 33% would use the treated risk as the denominator.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
RRR = ARR / control risk; always ask for the absolute figure.

---

items.question_text: A trial with no pre-specified subgroups reports a non-significant overall result. The authors then test 20 subgroups and highlight one in which p = 0.04, concluding the drug works in left-handed women. What is the most important flaw?
options: The trial was not blinded
p = 0.04 proves a 96% chance the effect is real
Multiple comparisons: about one in 20 tests will be significant at p < 0.05 by chance alone
The p-value is too large to be meaningful
Subgroups always have more power than the main analysis
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Multiple comparisons: about one in 20 tests will be significant at p < 0.05 by chance alone

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A post hoc subgroup finding after a negative trial.

2. THE RULE
A 95% confidence interval that includes the null value is compatible with no effect, and a non-significant result in a small study may be a type II error.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
With 20 independent tests at α = 0.05, about one false-positive result is expected by chance. Unplanned subgroup findings after a negative main result are hypothesis-generating only and need confirmation, or correction for multiple testing.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. The trial was not blinded: Nothing in the stem suggests a blinding failure.
B. p = 0.04 proves a 96% chance the effect is real: A p-value is not the probability that the effect is real.
D. The p-value is too large to be meaningful: p = 0.04 is below 0.05; the problem is how many tests were done.
E. Subgroups always have more power than the main analysis: Subgroups have less power, not more.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Many comparisons create chance 'significant' results.

---

items.question_text: After a screening test for a cancer is introduced, incidence of the cancer rises sharply and five-year survival improves, but the death rate from the cancer in the population does not change. Many of the extra cancers found are small and indolent. Which explanation best fits this pattern?
options: Regression to the mean
Selection bias from healthy volunteers only
Confounding by smoking
Overdiagnosis of cancers that would never have caused harm
Screening has reduced cancer deaths
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Overdiagnosis of cancers that would never have caused harm

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Rising incidence and survival with unchanged mortality after screening.

2. THE RULE
Lead-time and length-time biases can make screening look beneficial for survival without delaying death.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Overdiagnosis is the detection of disease that would never have caused symptoms or death. It increases incidence and improves apparent survival without reducing mortality, as seen with some thyroid and prostate cancer screening. Mortality is the key outcome.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Regression to the mean: Regression to the mean concerns repeated measurements of extreme values.
B. Selection bias from healthy volunteers only: Healthy volunteer bias affects comparisons of participants with non-participants, not population incidence.
C. Confounding by smoking: Smoking is not suggested as a confounder here.
E. Screening has reduced cancer deaths: Unchanged mortality shows no reduction in deaths.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Overdiagnosis raises incidence and survival but not mortality.

---

items.question_text: Without screening, a cancer is diagnosed at age 66 and the patient dies at 70. With screening, the same cancer is found at age 63 and the patient still dies at 70. A report says screening increased survival after diagnosis. What explains the apparent improvement?
options: True benefit of 3 extra years of life
Lead-time bias: survival appears 3 years longer although the age at death is unchanged
Attrition bias
Length-time bias
Overdiagnosis
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Lead-time bias: survival appears 3 years longer although the age at death is unchanged

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Earlier diagnosis with an unchanged age at death.

2. THE RULE
Lead-time and length-time biases can make screening look beneficial for survival without delaying death.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Survival measured from diagnosis is 4 years without screening and 7 years with screening, but death occurs at 70 in both cases. Earlier diagnosis alone adds 3 years of apparent survival (the lead time) without extending life.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. True benefit of 3 extra years of life: Age at death is unchanged, so no life is gained.
C. Attrition bias: No loss to follow-up is described.
D. Length-time bias: Length-time bias concerns preferential detection of slower-growing tumours.
E. Overdiagnosis: The cancer would have caused symptoms; it is not overdiagnosed.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Lead time lengthens survival from diagnosis without delaying death.

items.question_text: In a trial, sequentially numbered sealed envelopes were used for allocation. An audit finds that recruiters held envelopes up to the light and enrolled sicker patients when the next envelope showed the control arm. Outcome assessors were blinded. What is the main problem?
options: Loss to follow-up
Failure of outcome assessor blinding
Lack of intention-to-treat analysis
Contamination between arms
Failure of allocation concealment, causing selection bias
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Failure of allocation concealment, causing selection bias

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Recruiters could see the next allocation.

2. THE RULE
Intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in their allocated group, and allocation concealment differs from blinding.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
Allocation concealment prevents recruiters from knowing the next assignment before enrolment. Once it is broken, recruiters can steer patients and the groups differ at baseline (selection bias), even with later blinding. Opaque envelopes or central randomisation prevent this.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Loss to follow-up: No loss to follow-up is described.
B. Failure of outcome assessor blinding: Assessors were blinded; the problem is before allocation.
C. Lack of intention-to-treat analysis: ITT concerns analysis after allocation.
D. Contamination between arms: Contamination is control patients receiving the intervention.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Allocation concealment protects randomisation before enrolment; blinding comes after.

---

items.question_text: A randomised trial compares laparoscopic and open hernia repair. Surgeons and patients obviously cannot be blinded to the procedure. The primary outcome is recurrence on clinical examination at 2 years. Which design feature best reduces bias in measuring the outcome?
options: Blinded outcome assessors who do not know which repair was done
Using a placebo operation for both groups
Letting the operating surgeon assess recurrence
Per-protocol analysis only
Abandoning randomisation because blinding is impossible
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Blinded outcome assessors who do not know which repair was done

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A surgical trial where participants cannot be blinded.

2. THE RULE
Intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in their allocated group, and allocation concealment differs from blinding.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
When participants and surgeons cannot be blinded, independent outcome assessors unaware of allocation reduce detection bias. Randomisation and allocation concealment still protect against selection bias.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Using a placebo operation for both groups: A sham operation would not be ethical or practical here.
C. Letting the operating surgeon assess recurrence: The operating surgeon has a strong bias.
D. Per-protocol analysis only: Per-protocol analysis increases bias; ITT is preferred.
E. Abandoning randomisation because blinding is impossible: Randomisation remains essential even without blinding.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
If participants cannot be blinded, blind the outcome assessors.

---

items.question_text: A study compares 30 countries and finds that those with higher average salt intake have higher stroke death rates. A newspaper concludes that any individual who eats more salt will have a stroke. What is the main limitation?
options: Ecological fallacy: a group-level association may not apply to individuals
Lead-time bias
Lack of a placebo
Recall bias from salt questionnaires
Loss to follow-up
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Ecological fallacy: a group-level association may not apply to individuals

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Country-level data used to draw conclusions about individuals.

2. THE RULE
Study design determines what can be estimated: case-control studies give odds ratios, cohorts give incidence, and cross-sectional studies cannot show temporal direction.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
This is an ecological study using country-level data. Associations between averages do not show that the individuals with high intake are the ones who have strokes. It generates hypotheses for individual-level studies.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Lead-time bias: Lead-time bias applies to screening survival comparisons.
C. Lack of a placebo: Observational studies have no placebo by design.
D. Recall bias from salt questionnaires: The data are national averages, not individual recall.
E. Loss to follow-up: The study did not follow individuals.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Ecological studies cannot be applied directly to individuals.

---

items.question_text: An observational study finds that people prescribed a new inhaler had more hospital admissions than those on an older inhaler. The new inhaler is mainly prescribed by specialists to patients with severe asthma. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The new inhaler causes admissions
Measurement bias from blinded assessors
Lead-time bias
Confounding by indication: disease severity influences both the prescription and the outcome
Recall bias
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Confounding by indication: disease severity influences both the prescription and the outcome

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Sicker patients receive the new drug in an observational study.

2. THE RULE
A confounder is linked to both exposure and outcome and distorts the association, and unmeasured confounders can persist after adjustment.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Confounding by indication occurs when the reason for prescribing (severity) is itself associated with the outcome. Sicker patients receive the new treatment and are admitted more often. It is addressed by randomisation or careful adjustment for severity.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. The new inhaler causes admissions: Causation cannot be inferred while severity is uncontrolled.
B. Measurement bias from blinded assessors: Blinded assessment reduces bias rather than causing it.
C. Lead-time bias: Lead-time bias applies to screening.
E. Recall bias: Admissions are recorded events, not recalled.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Confounding by indication: the reason for treatment drives the outcome.

---

items.question_text: A cohort study examines whether obesity increases the risk of myocardial infarction. The researchers adjust for blood pressure, LDL cholesterol and diabetes, and the association almost disappears. They conclude that obesity does not cause heart attacks. What is the main error?
options: Obesity cannot be a confounder
They failed to adjust for blood pressure
They should have used an ecological design
The study is too large
Adjusting for mediators on the causal pathway removes part of the true effect of obesity
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Adjusting for mediators on the causal pathway removes part of the true effect of obesity

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Adjusting for mediators in a cohort study.

2. THE RULE
A confounder is linked to both exposure and outcome and distorts the association, and unmeasured confounders can persist after adjustment.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
Blood pressure, LDL and diabetes lie partly on the causal pathway between obesity and MI (they are mediators). Adjusting for them estimates only the direct effect, so the total effect is underestimated. A confounder is a common cause, not a step on the pathway.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Obesity cannot be a confounder: The question is about obesity as an exposure, and mediators are the error.
B. They failed to adjust for blood pressure: They did adjust for it; that is the problem.
C. They should have used an ecological design: An ecological design would be weaker.
D. The study is too large: Size is not the issue.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Do not adjust for mediators when estimating a total causal effect.

---

items.question_text: A case-control study of a rare cancer (lifetime risk under 1%) reports an odds ratio of 3.0 for an occupational exposure. A student says odds ratios can never be read as relative risks. What is the most accurate interpretation?
options: The OR overstates the relative risk tenfold
Because the outcome is rare, the OR approximates the relative risk, so exposure roughly triples the risk
Case-control studies give incidence directly
The relative risk is exactly 1/3
The OR cannot say anything about risk
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Because the outcome is rare, the OR approximates the relative risk, so exposure roughly triples the risk

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Interpreting an OR for a rare outcome.

2. THE RULE
When the outcome is common, the odds ratio overstates the relative risk, so cohort data should report the relative risk.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
When the outcome is rare (under about 10%), the odds approximate the risk, so the odds ratio approximates the relative risk (the rare disease assumption). This is why case-control studies of rare diseases estimate relative risk well.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. The OR overstates the relative risk tenfold: Divergence matters when the outcome is common.
C. Case-control studies give incidence directly: Case-control studies cannot measure incidence directly.
D. The relative risk is exactly 1/3: The direction of effect is not reversed.
E. The OR cannot say anything about risk: The rare disease assumption allows the OR to approximate the RR.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
For rare outcomes, OR ≈ RR.

---

items.question_text: In a case-control study, 40 of 100 cases and 20 of 100 controls were exposed. What is the odds ratio?
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. 2.67

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Calculating an odds ratio from a 2 × 2 table.

2. THE RULE
When the outcome is common, the odds ratio overstates the relative risk, so cohort data should report the relative risk.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Odds of exposure in cases = 40/60 = 0.667. Odds in controls = 20/80 = 0.25. OR = 0.667 / 0.25 = 2.67, equivalent to (40 × 80) / (60 × 20) = 3200/1200.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. 4.0: 4.0 would require different cell counts.
B. 1.5: 1.5 has no derivation from these data.
D. 2.0: 2.0 is the ratio of proportions exposed (40% / 20%), not odds.
E. 0.375: 0.375 is the inverse of the correct OR.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
OR = (a × d) / (b × c).

items.question_text: A 74-year-old man on a surgical ward develops hyperactive delirium from a urinary infection on day 2 after admission. He needs a non-urgent decision about elective hernia repair, which can safely wait several weeks. His daughter, his enduring guardian, asks to sign the consent today while he is confused. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Accept the daughter's consent today
Ask the patient to sign during a lucid moment on the ward round today
Apply to the tribunal for an order authorising surgery
Proceed because he lacks capacity
Treat the delirium and defer the elective decision until he regains capacity
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Treat the delirium and defer the elective decision until he regains capacity

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A non-urgent decision during reversible delirium.

2. THE RULE
Capacity is decision- and time-specific; a diagnosis such as dementia does not remove it, and a substitute decision-maker acts only when capacity is lost.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
Capacity is time-specific. Delirium is usually reversible, and a substitute decision-maker should not decide a non-urgent matter that the person is likely to be able to decide for himself soon. The infection is treated and the elective decision deferred until capacity returns.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Accept the daughter's consent today: A substitute decision is not needed for a non-urgent matter while recovery is expected.
B. Ask the patient to sign during a lucid moment on the ward round today: A brief lucid moment during active delirium is not a sound basis for elective consent.
C. Apply to the tribunal for an order authorising surgery: A tribunal order is unnecessary when the decision can wait.
D. Proceed because he lacks capacity: Lack of capacity does not authorise elective surgery.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
If capacity is likely to return and the decision can wait, wait.

---

items.question_text: A 30-year-old woman with a moderate intellectual disability lives in supported accommodation. She asks for the contraceptive implant. With easy-read material and time, she can explain that it stops pregnancy, that her arm may be sore and bleeding may change, and that it can be removed. Her support worker says people with her diagnosis cannot consent. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Accept her own consent: with support she has capacity for this decision
Ask the support worker to consent on her behalf
Obtain consent from her guardian because of her diagnosis
Defer until a psychiatrist formally assesses her IQ
Refuse the implant until a tribunal decides
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Accept her own consent: with support she has capacity for this decision

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
An adult with intellectual disability making a contraceptive decision with support.

2. THE RULE
Capacity is decision- and time-specific; a diagnosis such as dementia does not remove it, and a substitute decision-maker acts only when capacity is lost.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Capacity is decision-specific and presumed in adults. A diagnosis of intellectual disability does not remove it. With supported decision-making (easy-read material, time), she understands, retains, weighs and communicates the decision, so she can consent herself.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Ask the support worker to consent on her behalf: Support workers cannot consent for a competent adult.
C. Obtain consent from her guardian because of her diagnosis: A diagnosis does not determine capacity.
D. Defer until a psychiatrist formally assesses her IQ: IQ testing is not a test of decision-specific capacity.
E. Refuse the implant until a tribunal decides: No tribunal is needed when the person has capacity.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Supported decision-making: capacity is decision-specific, not diagnosis-based.

---

items.question_text: A 31-year-old woman in labour at 39 weeks has a fetal heart trace with late decelerations. The obstetrician recommends an emergency caesarean section. She understands that her baby may die or be disabled without it, can weigh this, and refuses because of a previous traumatic birth. She has no mental illness. The registrar suggests overriding her for the baby's sake. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Proceed with caesarean section to protect the fetus
Seek an urgent court order to operate
Ask her partner to consent instead
Respect her informed refusal, keep exploring her concerns and offering options, and document carefully
Sedate her and proceed
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Respect her informed refusal, keep exploring her concerns and offering options, and document carefully

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A competent woman in labour refuses a recommended caesarean.

2. THE RULE
A competent adult's informed refusal of treatment must be respected and documented, even when family or clinicians disagree.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
In Australian law a competent pregnant woman may refuse treatment, including a caesarean, even if the fetus may be harmed; the fetus has no separate legal rights before birth. Clinicians should continue to discuss, address fears, offer alternatives and document, but cannot operate without consent.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Proceed with caesarean section to protect the fetus: Operating on a competent refusing patient is battery.
B. Seek an urgent court order to operate: Courts will not override a competent adult's refusal on behalf of a fetus.
C. Ask her partner to consent instead: A partner cannot consent for a competent adult.
E. Sedate her and proceed: Sedation to impose surgery is assault.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
A competent pregnant woman's refusal is binding, even if the fetus is at risk.

---

items.question_text: A 68-year-old man with a perforated bowel refuses surgery. When asked to explain, he says he believes the operation would leave him with a permanent bag 'for sure' and that he would rather die. The surgeon actually expects a temporary stoma that will probably be reversed. He is not delirious. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Accept the refusal as final and document it
Correct the misunderstanding with accurate information, then reassess whether his refusal is informed
Wait until he loses consciousness and then operate
Operate because his refusal is irrational
Call his son to consent instead
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Correct the misunderstanding with accurate information, then reassess whether his refusal is informed

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A refusal based on a factual misunderstanding.

2. THE RULE
A competent adult's informed refusal of treatment must be respected and documented, even when family or clinicians disagree.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
A refusal must be informed. Before accepting it, the clinician must check that the person has accurate information about the material facts. Here he holds a mistaken belief about a permanent stoma. Correct it, check understanding, and then respect his decision if he still refuses with capacity.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Accept the refusal as final and document it: Accepting it now would rest on wrong information.
C. Wait until he loses consciousness and then operate: Deliberately waiting for loss of consciousness undermines his autonomy.
D. Operate because his refusal is irrational: A decision that seems unwise is not the same as lacking capacity.
E. Call his son to consent instead: A relative cannot consent for an adult with capacity.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Correct misunderstandings before accepting a refusal as informed.

---

items.question_text: A 16-year-old boy in Adelaide wants a hepatitis A and typhoid vaccine before a school trip. He understands the risks and benefits. His father phones to say he objects to all vaccines and that no one under 18 can consent without a parent. What is the most appropriate response?
options: His father's objection overrides him until he is 18
A court order is needed before vaccinating
In South Australia a person aged 16 or over can consent to their own treatment as an adult, so vaccinate with his consent
He needs two doctors to certify his maturity
Vaccinate only if his mother agrees
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. In South Australia a person aged 16 or over can consent to their own treatment as an adult, so vaccinate with his consent

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A 16-year-old in South Australia consents against a parent's wishes.

2. THE RULE
A minor who is Gillick competent for the decision can consent to their own treatment.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Under the Consent to Medical Treatment and Palliative Care Act 1995 (SA) s 6, a person aged 16 or over may consent to medical treatment as if an adult. Below 16 in SA, a minor can consent if a doctor considers them capable and a second doctor agrees in writing. He is 16 and understands, so his consent suffices.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. His father's objection overrides him until he is 18: Parental objection does not override a 16-year-old's consent in SA.
B. A court order is needed before vaccinating: No court is needed.
D. He needs two doctors to certify his maturity: The two-doctor requirement applies under 16 in SA.
E. Vaccinate only if his mother agrees: The other parent's agreement is not required.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
In SA, people aged 16 and over consent as adults.

---

items.question_text: A 13-year-old girl with complex congenital heart disease is offered a high-risk elective valve operation. She says she wants it 'so I can play netball', but cannot describe the main risks, the alternatives or what recovery involves, even after explanation. Her parents support surgery. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: She is not competent for this decision; obtain parental consent while involving her in the discussion
Require a court order because she is a minor
Defer until she is 18
Accept her consent because she agrees
Accept her consent because she is over 12
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. She is not competent for this decision; obtain parental consent while involving her in the discussion

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A young adolescent who cannot grasp a complex decision.

2. THE RULE
A minor who is Gillick competent for the decision can consent to their own treatment.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Gillick competence is decision-specific: it depends on understanding the nature, risks and alternatives of the particular treatment. She cannot do this for a complex, high-risk operation, so a parent consents, while her views are heard and she is involved as far as possible.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Require a court order because she is a minor: Parents can consent to treatment in the child's best interests.
C. Defer until she is 18: Delaying a recommended elective operation for years is not necessary.
D. Accept her consent because she agrees: Agreement is not the same as competence.
E. Accept her consent because she is over 12: There is no fixed age that confers competence.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Gillick competence is decision-specific; complex decisions need deeper understanding.

---

items.question_text: A 35-year-old man tells you, calmly, that he has bought a knife and will kill his former partner tonight when she collects their child; he names her and her address. He refuses help and asks you to keep this confidential. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Book him a review next week
Keep the conversation confidential
Write a note in the file only
Disclose to police now to prevent a serious and imminent threat to an identifiable person
Wait for his consent before acting
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Disclose to police now to prevent a serious and imminent threat to an identifiable person

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A patient discloses a specific plan to kill a named person.

2. THE RULE
Confidentiality may be breached to prevent serious harm to an identifiable person, but not for curiosity, family requests or media interest, including after death.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Confidentiality can be breached when a doctor reasonably believes disclosure is necessary to lessen or prevent a serious threat to the life, health or safety of an individual (Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), permitted general situations and APP 6; state health records laws; Medical Board Good Medical Practice). A specific plan, a means, a named victim and a time justify informing police.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Book him a review next week: Delay could cost a life.
B. Keep the conversation confidential: Confidentiality is not absolute when life is threatened.
C. Write a note in the file only: Documentation alone does not prevent harm.
E. Wait for his consent before acting: Waiting for consent he has refused leaves her at risk.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
A serious, imminent threat to an identifiable person justifies disclosure to police.

---

items.question_text: A 4-year-old has bruises on both ears and his upper arm. His mother says he fell off a couch. You are unsure; the injuries could be accidental but the pattern concerns you. You plan to report only once you have proof by arranging a skeletal survey through the family and speaking to the father. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Investigate until you have proof before reporting
Report only if the child discloses abuse
Wait to see whether new bruises appear
Ask the parents to explain the bruises in writing first
Report now; reasonable grounds for suspicion are enough, and the agency investigates
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Report now; reasonable grounds for suspicion are enough, and the agency investigates

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Suspicious bruising without certainty.

2. THE RULE
Suspected child abuse is reported promptly as a statutory duty; a child's request for secrecy, family objection or a threat of legal action does not stop it, and good-faith reports are protected.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
Mandatory reporting laws require a report when a doctor forms a belief on reasonable grounds (or suspicion, depending on the jurisdiction) that a child is at risk of significant harm. Proof is not required, and it is the child protection agency's role to investigate. Bruising to the ears in a young child is a recognised warning sign.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Investigate until you have proof before reporting: Doctors are not required to prove abuse before reporting.
B. Report only if the child discloses abuse: A disclosure is not required.
C. Wait to see whether new bruises appear: Waiting exposes the child to further harm.
D. Ask the parents to explain the bruises in writing first: Questioning the family can increase risk to the child.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Report on reasonable suspicion; investigation is the agency's job.

---
